nodes.summary: A partial recursive code $c$ accepts a natural number $n$ when $c$ halts on input $n$ with output $0$. Acceptance is a predicate on pairs $(c, n)$; it is the analogue of Sipser's $A_{\mathrm{TM}}$, where a machine may halt without accepting.
nodes.title: Acceptance by a code

nodes.summary: For a pair $q = (c, n)$ of a partial recursive code and a natural number, let $g_q$ be the partial function on $\mathbb{N}$ that on input $x$ halts with output $0$ if $x$ is a perfect square, and otherwise runs $c$ on $n$ and, if that halts, outputs $0$ (and is undefined if it does not). Write $\ulcorner q \urcorner$ for the standard encoding of $q$ as a natural number, and $\langle a, b \rangle$ for the standard…
nodes.title: A single code for the regularity reduction function

nodes.summary: There is a partial recursive code $z$ that on input $0$ halts with output $0$ and on every input $x \ne 0$ does not halt.
nodes.title: A code that halts only on zero

nodes.summary: There is a multi-stack machine $M$, with a bijection between its input alphabet and the Booleans, such that no multi-stack machine decides, for $n \in \mathbb{N}$, whether $M$ halts when started on the binary representation of $n$ (written in $M$'s input alphabet through the bijection).
nodes.title: Some multi-stack machine has an undecidable halting set

nodes.summary: A partial recursive code $c$ halts on a natural number $n$ when its evaluation at $n$ is defined. Halting is a predicate on pairs $(c, n)$; it is the analogue of Sipser's $\mathrm{HALT}_{\mathrm{TM}}$.
nodes.title: Halting of a code on an input

nodes.summary: Say a partial recursive code $c$ accepts a natural number $n$ when $c$ halts on input $n$ with output $0$. Acceptance many-one reduces to halting: there is a computable map $f$ from pairs $(c, n)$ of a partial recursive code and a natural number to such pairs, such that for every pair $(c, n)$, the code $c$ accepts $n$ if and only if, writing $f(c, n) = (c', n')$, the code $c'$ halts on $n'$.
nodes.title: Acceptance reduces to halting

nodes.summary: Say a partial recursive code $c$ accepts a natural number $n$ when $c$ halts on input $n$ with output $0$. Halting many-one reduces to acceptance: there is a computable map $f$ from pairs $(c, n)$ of a partial recursive code and a natural number to such pairs, such that for every pair $(c, n)$, the code $c$ halts on $n$ if and only if, writing $f(c, n) = (c', n')$, the code $c'$ accepts $n'$.
nodes.title: Halting reduces to acceptance

nodes.summary: There is a computable map $f$ from pairs $(c, n)$ of a partial recursive code and a natural number to partial recursive codes such that for every pair $(c, n)$, the code $c$ halts on $n$ if and only if the halting set of $f(c, n)$ (the set of inputs on which it halts), read as a unary language, is regular. That is, halting many-one reduces to regularity of halting sets.
nodes.title: Halting reduces to regularity of halting sets

nodes.summary: Let $p$ and $q$ be predicates on primitive recursively encodable types $\alpha$ and $\beta$, and write $\langle x \rangle \in \mathbb{N}$ for the code of $x$. Then $p$ is many-one reducible to $q$ if and only if there is a function $f : \alpha \to \beta$ with $p(a) \iff q(f(a))$ for all $a \in \alpha$, together with a function $F : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ that a multi-stack machine computes on binary…
nodes.title: Mapping reductions are computed by multi-stack machines

nodes.summary: The unary language of the perfect squares, the set of words over a one-letter alphabet whose length is $m^2$ for some $m \in \mathbb{N}$, is not regular.
nodes.title: The unary squares are not regular

nodes.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the set of partial recursive codes whose program halts on input $n$ is not co-recognizable by a multi-stack machine: no multi-stack machine halts on exactly the codes whose program does not halt on input $n$.
nodes.title: The halting problem is not co-recognizable by multi-stack machines

nodes.summary: No multi-stack Turing machine decides, for pairs $(c, n)$ of a partial recursive code and a natural number, whether $c$ accepts $n$, that is, halts on $n$ with output $0$.
nodes.title: Acceptance is undecidable

nodes.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, no multi-stack machine decides whether a partial recursive code halts on input $n$.
nodes.title: The halting problem is undecidable by multi-stack machines

nodes.summary: No multi-stack Turing machine decides, for pairs $(c, n)$ of a partial recursive code and a natural number, whether $c$ halts on $n$.
nodes.title: Halting is undecidable

nodes.summary: Let $P$ be a set of subsets of $\mathbb{N}$, and suppose there are partial recursive codes $c_1$ and $c_2$ such that the domain of $c_1$ (the set of inputs on which it halts) belongs to $P$ and the domain of $c_2$ does not. Then the property of a partial recursive code $c$ that the domain of $c$ belongs to $P$ is not decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine.
nodes.title: Rice's theorem for languages

nodes.summary: Let $C$ be a set of partial functions $\mathbb{N} \rightharpoonup \mathbb{N}$, and suppose there are partial recursive functions $f \in C$ and $g \notin C$. Then the property of a partial recursive code $c$ that the partial function computed by $c$ belongs to $C$ is not decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine.
nodes.title: Rice's theorem for partial recursive codes

nodes.summary: For a partial recursive code $c$, let $\operatorname{dom}(c) \subseteq \mathbb{N}$ be the set of inputs on which $c$ halts. The property of $c$ that the unary language $\{w \in \{\ast\}^* : |w| \in \operatorname{dom}(c)\}$ is regular is not decidable by a multi-stack Turing machine.
nodes.title: Regularity of halting sets is undecidable

nodes.summary: A partial recursive code $c$ has a regular halting set when the unary language of its domain (the set of inputs on which $c$ halts), that is, the language of the words over a one-letter alphabet whose length lies in the domain of $c$, is regular.
nodes.title: Codes with a regular halting set

nodes.summary: For a partial recursive code $c$ and natural numbers $n$ and $x$, the value at $((c, n), x)$ is $0$ if $x$ is a perfect square; otherwise it is defined exactly when $c$ halts on input $n$, and then it is $0$.
nodes.title: Partial function of the halting-to-regularity reduction

nodes.summary: Let $C$ be a set of partial functions $\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$. If a multi-stack machine decides, for each partial recursive code, whether the function the code computes lies in $C$, then for all partial recursive functions $f$ and $g$, $f \in C$ implies $g \in C$.
nodes.title: Rice's theorem for multi-stack machines

nodes.summary: Let $p$ and $q$ be predicates on primitive recursively encodable types $\alpha$ and $\beta$. If $p$ is many-one reducible to $q$ and $q$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine, then $p$ is decidable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Decidability transfers along mapping reductions

nodes.summary: For every $n \in \mathbb{N}$, the set of partial recursive codes whose program halts on input $n$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: The halting problem is recognizable by multi-stack machines

nodes.summary: Let $p$ and $q$ be predicates on primitive recursively encodable types $\alpha$ and $\beta$. If $p$ is many-one reducible to $q$ and $q$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine, then $p$ is recognizable by a multi-stack machine.
nodes.title: Recognizability transfers along mapping reductions

nodes.summary: For a set $S \subseteq \mathbb{N}$, the unary language of $S$ is the language over the one-letter alphabet $\{\ast\}$ consisting of the words whose length lies in $S$.
nodes.title: Unary language of a set of naturals

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
